solas_davits.name: Boats For All Signed

drill.label: Order Full Boat Drill For The Crew

description.text: Her crew have never practised lowering the boats.
Every man of the deck crew has practised lowering the boats.
There are not enough seats in the boats.
There are lifeboat seats for everyone aboard.

description: In London the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea is signed. Born of the Titanic disaster, it requires a lifeboat place for everyone aboard.

description.text: Cunard adds collapsible boats to the Lusitania until she carries 48, enough for all.
No one requires her crew to practise launching them, and many of the deckhands taken on to replace men gone to war have never lowered a boat.

munitions_manifest.name: The Supplementary Manifest

offload.label: Have The Cartridge Cases Struck From The Cargo

description.text: The cartridges and shells sail in her forward holds.
The munitions are struck from the cargo and left on the pier.

description: At Pier 54 the Lusitania loads cargo for Liverpool. A supplementary manifest will be filed only after she sails.

description.text: It lists some 4,200 cases of rifle cartridges and 1,250 cases of shrapnel shells, stowed in the forward holds.
Whether any of it could explode will be argued over for a century.

embassy_warning.name: The Embassy Notice

publish.label: Run The Notice Beside The Sailing Advertisement

description.text: Few passengers take the notice seriously.
The notice is taken seriously, and many passengers cancel their passage.

description: The Imperial German Embassy publishes a notice in the New York papers: travellers sailing in the war zone on British ships do so at their own risk.

description.text: In several papers it runs directly beside Cunard’s advertisement for the Lusitania’s sailing.
Most passengers laugh it off. The Lusitania, they are told, is too fast for any submarine.

new_york_departure.name: She Clears Pier 54

hold.label: Hold The Sailing For Naval Escort

description.text: She sails without an escort.
Her sailing is held until the Navy can escort her.
She sails with nearly two thousand aboard.
Many passengers have cancelled, and she sails half empty.

description: Delayed two hours to take on passengers from the requisitioned Cameronia, the Lusitania leaves New York at 12:20.

description.text: Among her passengers are the millionaire Alfred Vanderbilt and the theatre producer Charles Frohman.
No escort is asked for and none is offered. Her speed is thought protection enough.

boiler_room_four.name: The Cold Boiler Room

relight.label: Relight No. 4 And Give Her All Twenty-Five Knots

description.text: Boiler room No. 4 stays cold.
All four boiler rooms are fired.
Her best speed is 21 knots.
She can make her full 25 knots.

description: To save coal and men on the wartime run, one of her four boiler rooms has been shut down. Instead of 25 knots she makes 21.

description.text: Cunard, losing money on the Atlantic service, counts on the saving to keep her sailing at all.
She is still faster than any submarine, but with little margin to escape one waiting ahead of her.

admiralty_warnings.name: Submarines Active Off The Coast

plot.label: Plot Every Sighting Onto One Chart

escort.label: Detach Destroyers To Meet Her At The Fastnet

description.text: Sightings are passed on piecemeal and never put together.
Every sighting is on a single chart, and the danger zone is plain.
No destroyers are sent.
Destroyers are sent to meet her at the Fastnet.
She makes her landfall alone.
She makes her landfall under escort.

description: Through the night the Admiralty sends warnings by wireless: submarines are active off the south coast of Ireland.

description.text: A U-boat has sunk the Candidate and the Centurion off the Irish coast the day before. The warnings give Captain Turner no positions to steer around.
No warship is sent to meet her. The old cruiser Juno, the only ship on patrol nearby, has been recalled to Queenstown.

u20_patrol.name: U-20 Lines Up The Shot

description.text: U-20 never gets a shot at her.
The liner steams into a perfect firing position.

description: Low on fuel and with few torpedoes left, Kapitänleutnant Walther Schwieger sees a large four-funnelled steamer come up over the horizon.

description.text: She turns across U-20’s bow toward the land, bringing herself within range of a submerged boat that could never have caught her.
At 14:10 he fires a single torpedo from about 700 metres.
She passes out of range, and U-20 turns for home with her torpedoes unspent.

four_point_bearing.name: The Four-Point Bearing

zigzag.label: Put Her On A Zigzag And Keep Her There

abandon.label: Abandon The Bearing And Run For Queenstown

description.text: She holds a straight course.
She steers an irregular zigzag.
Turner holds her steady to take the bearing.
Turner gives up the bearing and runs for Queenstown.
Her course is steady and easy to predict.
Her course is hard for any submarine to predict.

description: Close to the Old Head of Kinsale, Captain William Turner holds a steady course to take a four-point bearing and fix his position.

description.text: The Admiralty has advised masters to zigzag and to keep well offshore. Turner wants to know exactly where he is before he makes for Liverpool.
For some forty minutes she steers a straight line at 18 knots, the easiest target she has been all voyage.
No torpedo touches her.
The torpedo strikes her starboard bow.
At 14:10 a lookout sees the wake of a torpedo racing in on the starboard bow. It strikes just behind the bridge.
At 14:10 the Lusitania steams past the Old Head of Kinsale on a clear afternoon, unharmed.
Through his periscope, Schwieger notes an unusually heavy detonation.
She stays nearly upright.
She heels hard to starboard within minutes.
Moments after the torpedo, a second, larger explosion tears through her from deep inside the bow.
The torpedo’s blast is the only one. Her forward holds stay intact and she settles slowly.
In the forward holds, crates, mail and cargo ride out a calm crossing.
She takes an immediate list to starboard, and her bow begins to go under.
Its cause will be argued over for a century: the cartridges in the hold, coal dust, or a bursting boiler.

wireless_sos.name: The Set Loses Its Power

rigPower.label: Rig The Emergency Battery To The Key

description.text: Nothing keeps the set alive when the power fails.
The emergency battery keeps the key sending.
Her call for help is lost.
Queenstown hears her call for help.

description: Wireless operator Robert Leith sends the distress call again and again: “Come at once, big list, 10 miles south Old Head Kinsale.”

description.text: Within minutes the ship’s main power fails, and with it the power to the set.
Rescue from Queenstown will come in time only if someone there hears her.

trim.label: Counterflood To Port And Bring Her Upright

description.text: She keeps her list.
Counterflooding brings her nearly upright.
Most of the boats are lost in the launching.
The boats are lowered safely and full.
With the ship still making way and listing hard, the crew struggle to lower the boats. Only six of forty-eight get away safely.
The boats go down steadily, one after another, and they are full.
Her forty-eight boats stay in their chocks, never needed.
To starboard the boats swing out far from the side. To port they swing in against the hull and snag on the rivets as they are lowered.
Several are tipped over by crewmen who have never handled a fall, spilling everyone in them into the sea.
She stays afloat.
She goes down off the Old Head of Kinsale.
Eighteen minutes after the torpedo struck, the Lusitania goes down by the bow off the Old Head of Kinsale.
The Lusitania rounds the Old Head of Kinsale and sets course for Liverpool.
She is longer than the sea there is deep, and her bow strikes the seabed while her stern is still in the air.

ready.label: Have Every Tender Under Steam Before Noon

description.text: The rescue craft must raise steam before they can sail.
The rescue craft are under steam and ready to sail.
Help arrives too late for most of those in the water.
Help arrives while most of those in the water are still alive.
From Queenstown a flotilla of tugs, trawlers and fishing boats sets out for the Old Head of Kinsale.
No call comes, and the tugs and trawlers at Queenstown stay at their moorings.
Most arrive hours after the sinking. Many of those they reach have already died of cold in the water.
The rescue craft reach the survivors while most of them are still alive.
Most of those aboard survive.
Most of those aboard are lost.
The civilian toll is far lighter.
Hundreds of civilian passengers, children among them, are dead.
Through the night the boats bring the living and the dead into Queenstown. Of 1,959 aboard, 1,198 have died.
The boats bring the living and the dead into Queenstown. The loss is heavy, but with so many passengers having stayed home, far fewer have died than might have.
The survivors land at Queenstown cold, shaken and alive. Very few have been lost.
The quays at Queenstown are quiet. There is no one to bring ashore.
Among the dead are 128 Americans. Across the Atlantic, the sinking hardens opinion against Germany.

mersey_inquiry.name: Lord Mersey Sits Again

evidence.label: Put The Bridge Log Into The Record

description.text: The bridge log never reaches the inquiry.
The bridge log is part of the record.
Turner is cleared.
Turner carries the blame for how his ship was handled.

description: Lord Mersey, who led the inquiry into the Titanic, opens the British inquiry into the loss of the Lusitania.

description.text: The Admiralty, anxious that its own warnings and instructions not become the story, presses the case that Captain Turner ignored them.
Mersey’s findings leave a shadow over Turner that follows him for the rest of his life.
Mersey clears Turner and lays the blame on the German government alone.
